0.title: Micah: What Does the LORD Require of You?

1.text: <sup>1</sup>The word of the LORD that came to Micah of Moresheth in the days of Jotham, Ahaz, and Hezekiah, kings of Judah, which he saw concerning Samaria and Jerusalem.<sup>2</sup>Hear, you peoples, all of you; pay attention, O earth, and all that is in it, and let the Lord GOD be a witness against you, the Lord from his holy temple.<sup>3</sup>For behold, the LORD is coming out of his place, and will come down and tread upon the high places of the earth.<sup>4</sup>And the mountains will melt under him, and the valleys will split open, like wax before the fire, like waters poured down a steep place.<sup>5</sup>All this is for the transgression of Jacob and for the sins of the house of Israel. What is the transgression of Jacob? Is it not Samaria? And what is the high place of Judah? Is it not Jerusalem?<sup>6</sup>Therefore I will make Samaria a heap in the open country, a place for planting vineyards, and I will pour down her stones into the valley and uncover her foundations.<sup>7</sup>All her carved images shall be beaten to pieces, all her wages shall be burned with fire, and all her idols I will lay waste, for from the fee of a prostitute she gathered them, and to the fee of a prostitute they shall return.<sup>8</sup>For this I will lament and wail; I will go stripped and naked; I will make lamentation like the jackals, and mourning like the ostriches.<sup>9</sup>For her wound is incurable, and it has come to Judah; it has reached to the gate of my people, to Jerusalem.<sup>10</sup>Tell it not in Gath; weep not at all; in Beth-le-aphrah roll yourselves in the dust.<sup>11</sup>Pass on your way, inhabitants of Shaphir, in nakedness and shame; the inhabitants of Zaanan do not come out; the lamentation of Beth-ezel shall take away from you its standing place.<sup>12</sup>For the inhabitants of Maroth wait anxiously for good, because disaster has come down from the LORD to the gate of Jerusalem.<sup>13</sup>Harness the steeds to the chariots, inhabitants of Lachish; it was the beginning of sin to the daughter of Zion, for in you were found the transgressions of Israel.<sup>14</sup>Therefore you shall give parting gifts to Moresheth-gath; the houses of Achzib shall be a deceitful thing to the kings of Israel.<sup>15</sup>I will again bring a conqueror to you, inhabitants of Mareshah; the glory of Israel shall come to Adullam.<sup>16</sup>Make yourselves bald and cut off your hair, for the children of your delight; make yourselves as bald as the eagle, for they shall go from you into exile.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–7 — A Witness Against His People
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Micah of Moresheth sees a word concerning Samaria and Jerusalem (v. 1). All peoples are summoned as the Lord GOD comes out of his place, and the mountains melt like wax before the fire (vv. 2-4). The cause is named: the transgression of Jacob, and its address is the two capitals (v. 5). Samaria will become a heap in the open country, her idols smashed (vv. 6-7).
verseByVerse.theology: God himself comes down to judge, and the sin of his people begins at the places they are proudest of.

verseByVerse.quote: The word of the LORD that came to Micah of Moresheth in the days of Jotham, Ahaz, and Hezekiah, kings of Judah, which he saw concerning Samaria and Jerusalem.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The word of the LORD that came to Micah of Moresheth in the days of Jotham, Ahaz, and Hezekiah, kings of Judah, which he saw concerning Samaria and Jerusalem.

Micah of Moresheth was a country man. Moresheth (called Moresheth-gath in verse 14) was a small town in the low hills southwest of Jerusalem, near the Philistine border, farming country a long way from the palace and the temple. That background shows all through his book: he knows what it is like when powerful men in the city take a farmer's field.

He preached in the days of three kings of Judah: Jotham, Ahaz, and Hezekiah, roughly the second half of the eighth century BC. That makes him a contemporary of Isaiah, who names the same kings (Isa 1:1), and of Hosea (Hos 1:1), and he comes just after Amos. Four prophets in one generation, and still the people would not listen.

His message concerns Samaria and Jerusalem, the capitals of the northern and southern kingdoms. Samaria would fall to Assyria in 722 BC, within Micah's own lifetime, and Jerusalem would be surrounded in 701.

One more thing should be said about this man at the start. A century later, when Jeremiah was on trial for his life for preaching against Jerusalem, the elders defended him by remembering Micah: Micah of Moresheth prophesied in the days of Hezekiah, and Hezekiah did not ... put him to death but repented, and God did relent of the disaster (Jer 26:18-19). A country preacher's sermon changed a king's heart and spared a city, and was still remembered a hundred years later.

verseByVerse.quote: Hear, you peoples, all of you; pay attention, O earth, and all that is in it, and let the Lord GOD be a witness against you, the Lord from his holy temple. For behold, the LORD is coming out of his place, and will come down and tread upon the high places of the earth. And the mountains will melt under him, and the valleys will split open, like wax before the fire, like waters poured down a steep place.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Hear, you peoples, all of you; pay attention, O earth, and all that is in it, and let the Lord GOD be a witness against you, the Lord from his holy temple.

The book opens like a courtroom. Hear, says the prophet, and he summons not just Israel but you peoples, all of you and the earth itself as the jury. (The ESV notes the Hebrew reads "all of them".) And who is the witness against the accused? The Lord GOD himself, speaking from his holy temple. When God is both witness and judge, the case is not in doubt.

For behold, the LORD is coming out of his place, and will come down and tread upon the high places of the earth.

And the mountains will melt under him, and the valleys will split open, like wax before the fire, like waters poured down a steep place.

God is coming out of his place. Picture a king rising from his throne to deal with something himself. And the world cannot bear it. Mountains, the most solid things people know, melt like wax before the fire; valleys tear open; rock runs downhill like water. The psalm says the same: The mountains melt like wax before the LORD (Ps 97:5).

This is the God we are dealing with. We speak easily of God's love, and rightly, but the Bible will not let us make him small or safe. If mountains cannot stand before him, neither can we, except through the One who stood in our place.

verseByVerse.quote: All this is for the transgression of Jacob and for the sins of the house of Israel. What is the transgression of Jacob? Is it not Samaria? And what is the high place of Judah? Is it not Jerusalem? Therefore I will make Samaria a heap in the open country, a place for planting vineyards, and I will pour down her stones into the valley and uncover her foundations. All her carved images shall be beaten to pieces, all her wages shall be burned with fire, and all her idols I will lay waste, for from the fee of a prostitute she gathered them, and to the fee of a prostitute they shall return.
verseByVerse.commentary:
All this is for the transgression of Jacob and for the sins of the house of Israel. What is the transgression of Jacob? Is it not Samaria? And what is the high place of Judah? Is it not Jerusalem?

Why is God coming down? Not because he is capricious, but for the transgression of Jacob. Then Micah asks two questions and gives two shocking answers. Where is the transgression of the north? Samaria, the capital. Where is the high place, the shrine, of the south? Jerusalem, the city of the temple.

Sin was flowing downhill from the centres of power and worship. The places that should have led the nation to God were leading it away. Corruption at the top always spreads, and when the church or its leaders go wrong, the damage runs through everything.

Therefore I will make Samaria a heap in the open country, a place for planting vineyards, and I will pour down her stones into the valley and uncover her foundations.

Samaria was built on a hill, ringed with strong walls. God says the city will be tipped down the slope until the bare foundations show and farmers plant vines where the streets used to be. It happened in 722 BC, when Assyria captured Samaria and carried Israel away (2 Kgs 17:6).

All her carved images shall be beaten to pieces, all her wages shall be burned with fire, and all her idols I will lay waste, for from the fee of a prostitute she gathered them, and to the fee of a prostitute they shall return.

The carved images and idols will be destroyed along with the city. The language of prostitution is used all through the prophets for unfaithfulness to God, and here it is also literal: the shrines of Canaan used prostitution in their worship, and the temple treasuries were enriched by it. What was gathered from filth will go back to filth. Whatever people build on idols returns to nothing.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 8–16 — A Lament over the Towns
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The prophet grieves: I will lament and wail; I will go stripped and naked, for the wound has come to Judah, reaching to the gate of my people (vv. 8-9). Then he names town after town in his own district as the invader advances (vv. 10-15), and ends, Make yourselves bald and cut off your hair, for the children of your delight, who will go into exile (v. 16).
verseByVerse.theology: God's messenger weeps over the judgment he announces, and judgment reaches the ordinary villages, not only the capitals.

verseByVerse.quote: For this I will lament and wail; I will go stripped and naked; I will make lamentation like the jackals, and mourning like the ostriches. For her wound is incurable, and it has come to Judah; it has reached to the gate of my people, to Jerusalem.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For this I will lament and wail; I will go stripped and naked; I will make lamentation like the jackals, and mourning like the ostriches.

Now the prophet does something we should not miss. He does not announce the judgment coolly. He breaks down. I will lament and wail, going stripped and naked, the dress of a prisoner of war or a mourner who has lost everything. He howls like the desert animals, like the jackals and the ostriches, whose cries carry across the night.

This is what distinguishes a true prophet from a bitter one. Micah says the hardest things in this book, and he weeps while he says them. Anyone who speaks God's warnings without grief should ask whether he has understood them.

For her wound is incurable, and it has come to Judah; it has reached to the gate of my people, to Jerusalem.

Samaria's wound is incurable, and the infection is spreading south. It has reached to the gate of Jerusalem. That is exactly what happened in 701 BC, when Sennacherib's army took the fortified cities of Judah and his officers stood outside Jerusalem's walls (2 Kgs 18:13, 17).

There is one wound that is not incurable, and it is not ours. Isaiah, preaching in the same years, saw the Servant who was pierced for our transgressions, and said, with his wounds we are healed (Isa 53:5).

verseByVerse.quote: Tell it not in Gath; weep not at all; in Beth-le-aphrah roll yourselves in the dust. Pass on your way, inhabitants of Shaphir, in nakedness and shame; the inhabitants of Zaanan do not come out; the lamentation of Beth-ezel shall take away from you its standing place. For the inhabitants of Maroth wait anxiously for good, because disaster has come down from the LORD to the gate of Jerusalem.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Tell it not in Gath; weep not at all; in Beth-le-aphrah roll yourselves in the dust.

Now comes a funeral march through Micah's own neighbourhood. The towns named in these verses are small places in the Shephelah, the low hill country where he grew up, and together they trace the line of an invading army moving toward Jerusalem. This is not a general warning about a distant disaster. It is a list of the villages where his friends lived.

Tell it not in Gath is a quotation. David said it when Saul and Jonathan died: Tell it not in Gath, publish it not in the streets of Ashkelon (2 Sam 1:20), meaning, do not let the enemy hear of our disgrace. In Beth-le-aphrah the people are told to roll yourselves in the dust, an act of deep mourning.

Pass on your way, inhabitants of Shaphir, in nakedness and shame; the inhabitants of Zaanan do not come out; the lamentation of Beth-ezel shall take away from you its standing place.

For the inhabitants of Maroth wait anxiously for good, because disaster has come down from the LORD to the gate of Jerusalem.

Town after town, the picture is the same: people marched away in nakedness and shame, others shut inside their walls, afraid to come out, others with no safe place left to stand. The people of Maroth wait anxiously for good that never comes.

And notice where the trouble originates: disaster has come down from the LORD. Assyrian soldiers will do the damage, but Micah will not let his hearers treat it as bad luck or mere politics.

verseByVerse.quote: Harness the steeds to the chariots, inhabitants of Lachish; it was the beginning of sin to the daughter of Zion, for in you were found the transgressions of Israel. Therefore you shall give parting gifts to Moresheth-gath; the houses of Achzib shall be a deceitful thing to the kings of Israel. I will again bring a conqueror to you, inhabitants of Mareshah; the glory of Israel shall come to Adullam. Make yourselves bald and cut off your hair, for the children of your delight; make yourselves as bald as the eagle, for they shall go from you into exile.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Harness the steeds to the chariots, inhabitants of Lachish; it was the beginning of sin to the daughter of Zion, for in you were found the transgressions of Israel.

Lachish was the second city of Judah, a great fortress guarding the road to Jerusalem, and a chariot base. It is called the beginning of sin to the daughter of Zion, probably because this was where Judah put its trust in horses and military strength instead of God, and where the idolatry of the north came south. In 701 BC Lachish became the Assyrian army's headquarters, and its fall was carved in stone on the walls of Sennacherib's palace (2 Kgs 18:14, 17).

Therefore you shall give parting gifts to Moresheth-gath; the houses of Achzib shall be a deceitful thing to the kings of Israel.

Now the prophet names his own home town, Moresheth-gath. The parting gifts (the ESV notes this may mean a dowry) are what a father gave a daughter when she left home for good. Micah's village is being handed over like a bride to a foreign power. He does not exempt his own people from the message.

I will again bring a conqueror to you, inhabitants of Mareshah; the glory of Israel shall come to Adullam.

Adullam was the cave country where David hid from Saul (1 Sam 22:1). The glory of Israel, the nation's leaders and wealth, will end up back in the caves where the kingdom began, as fugitives.

Make yourselves bald and cut off your hair, for the children of your delight; make yourselves as bald as the eagle, for they shall go from you into exile.

Shaving the head was a public sign of grief (Isa 22:12). The chapter ends with parents told to mourn as if at a funeral, because the children of your delight are going into exile. Sin is never private. It costs the next generation.

Yet remember how this book ends, and what Jeremiah's generation remembered about Micah. He preached judgment on Jerusalem, and a king listened and repented, and God relented (Jer 26:18-19). Warnings like this one are given so that they need not come true.

1.title: The LORD Comes Down
1.overview:
The word of the LORD comes to Micah of Moresheth in the days of Jotham, Ahaz and Hezekiah, concerning Samaria and Jerusalem (v. 1). All peoples and the earth itself are called to hear, with the Lord GOD as witness from his holy temple. He comes out of his place and treads on the heights, so that the mountains melt like wax and the valleys split open (vv. 2-4).

All this is for the transgression of Jacob, and Micah names the two capitals as the sites of that sin. Samaria will be made a heap in the open country, her stones poured into the valley and her foundations uncovered, her images broken and her idols destroyed, since what was gathered from a prostitute's fee returns to it (vv. 5-7).

The prophet laments, going stripped and naked, howling like jackals and ostriches, for Samaria's wound is incurable and has reached the gate of Jerusalem (vv. 8-9). He then names town after town of his own district as the invader advances: Gath, Beth-le-aphrah, Shaphir, Zaanan, Beth-ezel, Maroth, Lachish, Moresheth-gath, Achzib, Mareshah and Adullam (vv. 10-15). The chapter ends with a call to shave the head in mourning, for the children of their delight will go into exile (v. 16).
1.theology:
God summons the whole earth as witness and comes down himself to judge; no created thing can stand before him (vv. 2-4; Ps 97:5).

Sin is most serious where privilege is greatest, and corruption at the centres of power and worship spreads through a whole nation (v. 5).

What is built on idols and gained by filth returns to nothing (vv. 6-7).

God's messenger weeps over the judgment he must announce (v. 8).

Human wounds may be incurable, but Christ's wounds heal (v. 9; Isa 53:5).

God rules the disasters that human armies inflict; they are never mere politics (v. 12).

Trust in military strength is itself a sin, and it spreads (v. 13).

Sin costs the next generation, and warnings are given so that they need not be fulfilled (v. 16; Jer 26:18-19).
1.examples:
A country preacher from a farming town sent to accuse two capitals.

Mountains running downhill like wax before a fire.

A hilltop city tipped into the valley until its foundations show.

A prophet howling like a jackal over the message he has to deliver.

A funeral march through the villages where the preacher grew up.

Chariot horses harnessed in the town that trusted them.

A village handed over like a daughter leaving home for good.

Parents shaving their heads for children who will not come back.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–5 — Woe to Those Who Covet Fields
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Woe to those who devise wickedness and work evil on their beds! — men who covet fields and seize them because they have the power to do it (vv. 1-2). So God says, against this family I am devising disaster (v. 3). Their own taunt song will mourn the fields taken from them, and they will have none to cast the line by lot in the assembly of the LORD (vv. 4-5).
verseByVerse.theology: God answers those who plot against their neighbours by plotting against them.

verseByVerse.quote: Woe to those who devise wickedness and work evil on their beds! When the morning dawns, they perform it, because it is in the power of their hand. They covet fields and seize them, and houses, and take them away; they oppress a man and his house, a man and his inheritance.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Woe to those who devise wickedness and work evil on their beds! When the morning dawns, they perform it, because it is in the power of their hand.

Micah takes us into the bedrooms of the powerful. They lie awake on their beds, not tossing with guilt but planning: how to get that piece of land, how to structure the loan so the farmer cannot repay. At first light they get up and do it. And the reason they do it is chillingly simple: because it is in the power of their hand. They can, so they do.

That is one of the plainest definitions of wickedness in the Bible. Not "is this right?" but "can I get away with it?" Ask what your imagination does when it is free, at night, in the shower, on the commute. Sin is not only what we finally do; it is what we rehearse.

They covet fields and seize them, and houses, and take them away; they oppress a man and his house, a man and his inheritance.

Notice the chain: they covet, then they seize, then they take. The tenth commandment forbids the first step precisely because it leads to the others (Exod 20:17).

To an Israelite this was worse than theft. The land was not simply property; God had said, The land shall not be sold in perpetuity, for the land is mine (Lev 25:23), and each family's field was its God-given inheritance, its share in the promise. To take a man's field was to cut him out of what God had given him. Ahab did it to Naboth, who told him, The LORD forbid that I should give you the inheritance of my fathers (1 Kgs 21:3). Isaiah, preaching at the same time as Micah, cried, Woe to those who join house to house, who add field to field (Isa 5:8).

This still speaks wherever the strong use law, debt or paperwork to take from the weak what keeps them alive.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore thus says the LORD: behold, against this family I am devising disaster, from which you cannot remove your necks, and you shall not walk haughtily, for it will be a time of disaster. In that day they shall take up a taunt song against you and moan bitterly, and say, "We are utterly ruined; he changes the portion of my people; how he removes it from me! To an apostate he allots our fields." Therefore you will have none to cast the line by lot in the assembly of the LORD.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Therefore thus says the LORD: behold, against this family I am devising disaster, from which you cannot remove your necks, and you shall not walk haughtily, for it will be a time of disaster.

They devised wickedness on their beds; now God says, I am devising disaster. (The ESV notes that the word for disaster here is the same word used for evil, depending on the context, which makes the answer fit the crime exactly.) The plotters are out-plotted.

The picture is of a yoke laid on the neck of an ox: from which you cannot remove your necks. They have walked haughtily, heads high through the village, and they will not do it again.

In that day they shall take up a taunt song against you and moan bitterly, and say, "We are utterly ruined; he changes the portion of my people; how he removes it from me! To an apostate he allots our fields."

Here is a bitter irony. The men who took other people's fields will one day sing a funeral song about their own: To an apostate he allots our fields, meaning a foreign conqueror will carve up their land. What we take unjustly, we do not keep.

Therefore you will have none to cast the line by lot in the assembly of the LORD.

When Israel entered the land, each family's portion was measured out by lot. These men will have no one left to hold the measuring line for them. They have lost their place in the assembly of the LORD itself. Grabbing more and more of God's gifts, they end with no share at all in the Giver.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: "Do not preach"—thus they preach, and they ask whether God has grown impatient (vv. 6-7). Meanwhile they rob travellers, drive women from their homes and strip children of their inheritance (vv. 8-10). The preacher this people want is one who promises wine and strong drink (v. 11). Yet God promises to gather the remnant of Israel like a flock, and He who opens the breach goes up before them, with the LORD at their head (vv. 12-13).
verseByVerse.theology: People who silence God's word still have a future only because God keeps a remnant and goes before them himself.

verseByVerse.quote: "Do not preach"—thus they preach— "one should not preach of such things; disgrace will not overtake us." Should this be said, O house of Jacob? Has the LORD grown impatient? Are these his deeds? Do not my words do good to him who walks uprightly?
verseByVerse.commentary:
"Do not preach"—thus they preach— "one should not preach of such things; disgrace will not overtake us."

The people answer back, and the wording is almost comic: "Do not preach"—thus they preach. They have their own sermon, and its text is that nobody should say things like this. Their confidence is in a slogan: disgrace will not overtake us. Nothing bad can happen to people like us.

Every generation has this instinct. Say what you like about sin in general; do not name ours. Amos heard it at Bethel (Amos 7:13), and Paul warned Timothy of people who will not endure sound teaching (2 Tim 4:3).

Should this be said, O house of Jacob? Has the LORD grown impatient? Are these his deeds? Do not my words do good to him who walks uprightly?

God answers their complaint with questions. Has the LORD grown impatient? (The ESV notes the Hebrew reads "Has the spirit of the LORD grown short?") They are blaming the message on a bad mood in heaven, as though God had simply lost his temper.

Then the key sentence: Do not my words do good to him who walks uprightly? God's word is not harsh; it feels harsh to people who are living crookedly. The same sunlight that comforts healthy eyes hurts inflamed ones. If Scripture seems to us only negative and restrictive, the problem may not be with Scripture.

verseByVerse.quote: But lately my people have risen up as an enemy; you strip the rich robe from those who pass by trustingly with no thought of war. The women of my people you drive out from their delightful houses; from their young children you take away my splendor forever. Arise and go, for this is no place to rest, because of uncleanness that destroys with a grievous destruction. If a man should go about and utter wind and lies, saying, "I will preach to you of wine and strong drink," he would be the preacher for this people!
verseByVerse.commentary:
But lately my people have risen up as an enemy; you strip the rich robe from those who pass by trustingly with no thought of war.

God's own people have started behaving like an invading army. They strip travellers who pass by trustingly (the ESV notes this may be "returning from war"). People walking home in peace are robbed by their own countrymen.

The women of my people you drive out from their delightful houses; from their young children you take away my splendor forever.

Now the victims are named: widows and children. Women are evicted from their delightful houses, the homes their husbands left them, and the children lose my splendor, the dignity and inheritance God himself had given them. Note that word my. God calls their inheritance his own splendour. Rob a child of his future, and you are robbing God.

Arise and go, for this is no place to rest, because of uncleanness that destroys with a grievous destruction.

The promised land was meant to be the place of rest. Now God says this is no place to rest. A society that devours its weakest has made its own home uninhabitable, and exile is coming.

If a man should go about and utter wind and lies, saying, "I will preach to you of wine and strong drink," he would be the preacher for this people!

Here is the verdict on their religious taste. Send them a preacher who talks about wine and strong drink, plenty and good times, and they will pack the building. Wind and lies is what they want. Preaching that only ever promises prosperity and never mentions sin is not new, and it is not kindness; it leaves people comfortable on the way to ruin.

verseByVerse.quote: I will surely assemble all of you, O Jacob; I will gather the remnant of Israel; I will set them together like sheep in a fold, like a flock in its pasture, a noisy multitude of men. He who opens the breach goes up before them; they break through and pass the gate, going out by it. Their king passes on before them, the LORD at their head.
verseByVerse.commentary:
I will surely assemble all of you, O Jacob; I will gather the remnant of Israel; I will set them together like sheep in a fold, like a flock in its pasture, a noisy multitude of men.

Suddenly the tone changes completely. After all that judgment, God promises to gather the remnant of Israel. Some readers take these two verses as more judgment, a flock penned up ready to be driven away. But the words fit a rescue better: a pasture, a noisy multitude, a king going before them. Micah does this all through his book, turning without warning from the darkest threats to sudden promise, because judgment is never God's last word for his people.

Notice the word remnant. God does not promise to save everyone in that generation, but he will not lose his own. He will always have a people.

He who opens the breach goes up before them; they break through and pass the gate, going out by it. Their king passes on before them, the LORD at their head.

Picture a walled town where a flock is penned. Someone smashes an opening in the wall, and the sheep pour out after him into the open country. That is the image: He who opens the breach goes up before them. God's people are hemmed in, trapped by enemies and by their own history, and someone goes ahead of them and makes a way out.

Who is he? Micah gives two names in one line: Their king and the LORD at their head. The king who breaks the wall is God himself. Later in this book we will be told where that king is born (5:2).

Christians cannot read this without thinking of Jesus. He is the shepherd who calls his own sheep by name and leads them out, and goes before them (John 10:3-4). He broke open the way through death itself, going ahead as a forerunner on our behalf (Heb 6:20). Every believer who has ever been trapped by sin, guilt or fear should hear this verse: there is someone who goes first and makes an opening.

2.title: The Breaker Goes Up Before Them
2.overview:
Woe to those who lie on their beds devising wickedness and carry it out at daybreak simply because they have the power. They covet fields and seize them, houses and take them, oppressing a man and his inheritance (vv. 1-2). Therefore God is devising disaster against this family, a yoke they cannot shake off, and they will no longer walk haughtily (v. 3). In that day they will sing a bitter taunt song about their own fields being handed to an apostate, and they will have no one to cast the measuring line in the assembly of the LORD (vv. 4-5).

"Do not preach", they preach, insisting that disgrace will not overtake them. God asks whether he has grown impatient, and whether his words do not do good to those who walk uprightly (vv. 6-7). But his people have risen up like an enemy, stripping robes from trusting travellers, driving women from their homes and taking his splendour from their children, so the land is no place to rest (vv. 8-10). The preacher this people want is one who utters wind and lies and promises wine and strong drink (v. 11).

Yet God will surely assemble Jacob and gather the remnant of Israel like sheep in a fold. He who opens the breach goes up before them; they break through the gate and go out, their king before them and the LORD at their head (vv. 12-13).
2.theology:
Sin begins in the imagination, and power without conscience is its own justification (v. 1).

Property taken from the weak is taken from God, who gave each family its inheritance (vv. 2, 9; Lev 25:23; 1 Kgs 21:3).

God repays scheming with judgment that fits the crime, and what is grabbed unjustly is not kept (vv. 3-5).

God's word does good to the upright; it is only bitter to those who are living crookedly (v. 7).

People get the preachers they want, and comfortable preaching is not kindness (vv. 6, 11; 2 Tim 4:3).

God always preserves a remnant, and judgment is never his last word for his people (v. 12).

God himself goes before his people to break open a way out, fulfilled in Christ the shepherd-king and forerunner (v. 13; John 10:3-4; Heb 6:20).
2.examples:
Men lying awake planning how to take a neighbour's field.

A land grab carried out at first light because nobody can stop it.

Thieves singing a funeral song over their own stolen fields.

A congregation whose favourite sermon is "do not preach".

A widow put out of the house her husband left her.

A preacher of wine and good times, filling the building.

A wall broken open and a flock pouring out after its king.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–4 — Rulers Who Hate the Good
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Hear, you heads of Jacob and rulers of the house of Israel! Is it not for you to know justice? (v. 1). Instead they hate the good and love the evil, and Micah pictures them butchering their own people (vv. 2-3). When disaster comes and they cry to God, he will not answer them (v. 4).
verseByVerse.theology: Leaders exist to know and do justice, and God will not hear those who have devoured the people he gave them.

verseByVerse.quote: And I said: Hear, you heads of Jacob and rulers of the house of Israel! Is it not for you to know justice?— you who hate the good and love the evil, who tear the skin from off my people and their flesh from off their bones, who eat the flesh of my people, and flay their skin from off them, and break their bones in pieces and chop them up like meat in a pot, like flesh in a cauldron. Then they will cry to the LORD, but he will not answer them; he will hide his face from them at that time, because they have made their deeds evil.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And I said: Hear, you heads of Jacob and rulers of the house of Israel! Is it not for you to know justice?—

Micah turns from the wealthy to the leaders: the heads and rulers, the men who sat in the courts and ran the country. His question is almost gentle, and it cuts deep: Is it not for you to know justice? This is your job. It is the one thing you exist to do.

you who hate the good and love the evil, who tear the skin from off my people and their flesh from off their bones,

who eat the flesh of my people, and flay their skin from off them, and break their bones in pieces and chop them up like meat in a pot, like flesh in a cauldron.

The charge is that they have turned right round: they hate the good and love the evil. And then comes language of shocking violence. The rulers are butchers, skinning people, breaking their bones, chopping them up like meat in a pot. (The ESV notes that the Hebrew of one line reads "from off them".)

This is a picture, not a report of cannibalism. But it is a picture God chose. What these men were actually doing was taking land, charging ruinous interest, fixing court cases and keeping wages. In heaven's view, that is butchery. Remember that when injustice is discussed in the polite language of policy and markets; God describes it in the language of a slaughterhouse.

Then they will cry to the LORD, but he will not answer them; he will hide his face from them at that time, because they have made their deeds evil.

The day will come when these same men pray. And God will not answer them. Isaiah said it to the same generation: even though you make many prayers, I will not listen; your hands are full of blood (Isa 1:15). There is a kind of prayer God refuses, not because his ear is heavy, but because the one praying has no intention of changing. The door of mercy is wide, but it is not a way of avoiding consequences while keeping the sin.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The prophets cry "Peace" when they have something to eat, and declare war on anyone who does not feed them (v. 5). So their sun will go down and they will have no answer from God (vv. 6-7). Micah stands apart: I am filled with power, with the Spirit of the LORD (v. 8). Heads judge for a bribe, priests teach for a price, prophets divine for money, and all of them say, Is not the LORD in the midst of us? (vv. 9-11). Therefore Zion shall be plowed as a field (v. 12).
verseByVerse.theology: Ministry sold for money ends in silence from God, and religious confidence without obedience cannot save a city.

verseByVerse.quote: Thus says the LORD concerning the prophets who lead my people astray, who cry "Peace" when they have something to eat, but declare war against him who puts nothing into their mouths. Therefore it shall be night to you, without vision, and darkness to you, without divination. The sun shall go down on the prophets, and the day shall be black over them; the seers shall be disgraced, and the diviners put to shame; they shall all cover their lips, for there is no answer from God. But as for me, I am filled with power, with the Spirit of the LORD, and with justice and might, to declare to Jacob his transgression and to Israel his sin.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Thus says the LORD concerning the prophets who lead my people astray, who cry "Peace" when they have something to eat, but declare war against him who puts nothing into their mouths.

Now the preachers. Their message depends on the fee. Feed them, and they cry "Peace"; give them nothing, and they announce judgment on you. They have turned the word of God into a service industry, priced by the customer.

That is a searching word for anyone in paid ministry today. It does not condemn supporting ministers; Scripture commands it. It condemns letting the money shape the message: the sermon softened because a major giver is in the building, the sin never named because it is the sin of the people who pay the bills. Peter tells elders to serve not for shameful gain, but eagerly (1 Pet 5:2), and Paul says, we are not, like so many, peddlers of God's word (2 Cor 2:17).

Therefore it shall be night to you, without vision, and darkness to you, without divination. The sun shall go down on the prophets, and the day shall be black over them;

the seers shall be disgraced, and the diviners put to shame; they shall all cover their lips, for there is no answer from God.

The punishment fits exactly. They sold visions, so the visions stop. It shall be night to you: the sun goes down on men whose trade was light. They cover their lips, a sign of shame, because there is no answer from God. There are few more frightening judgments on a religious establishment than silence.

But as for me, I am filled with power, with the Spirit of the LORD, and with justice and might, to declare to Jacob his transgression and to Israel his sin.

But as for me. One man stands against the whole professional class, and he does not claim to be cleverer or better connected. He is filled with power, with the Spirit of the LORD. That is the only qualification that matters, and it is a gift.

See what the Spirit produces in him: justice and might, and the courage to declare to Jacob his transgression. The Spirit does not make him popular; he makes him truthful. The greater Prophet would one day stand in a synagogue and say, The Spirit of the Lord is upon me (Luke 4:18), and speak the truth at the cost of his life.

verseByVerse.quote: Hear this, you heads of the house of Jacob and rulers of the house of Israel, who detest justice and make crooked all that is straight, who build Zion with blood and Jerusalem with iniquity. Its heads give judgment for a bribe; its priests teach for a price; its prophets practice divination for money; yet they lean on the LORD and say, "Is not the LORD in the midst of us? No disaster shall come upon us." Therefore because of you Zion shall be plowed as a field; Jerusalem shall become a heap of ruins, and the mountain of the house a wooded height.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Hear this, you heads of the house of Jacob and rulers of the house of Israel, who detest justice and make crooked all that is straight,

who build Zion with blood and Jerusalem with iniquity.

They make crooked all that is straight: take a clear law and bend it until it serves them. And they build Zion with blood. The city was being beautified, and every fine new building was paid for by somebody's ruin. God looks at the architecture and sees the blood in the mortar.

Its heads give judgment for a bribe; its priests teach for a price; its prophets practice divination for money; yet they lean on the LORD and say, "Is not the LORD in the midst of us? No disaster shall come upon us."

Here is the whole leadership of the nation in one verse: judges, priests and prophets, and all three have a price. And then the astonishing last line. These same men lean on the LORD and say, Is not the LORD in the midst of us?

They were not atheists. They were orthodox. They had the temple, the sacrifices, the promises to David, and they treated all of it as insurance. Jeremiah met the same slogan a century later: Do not trust in these deceptive words: 'This is the temple of the LORD, the temple of the LORD, the temple of the LORD' (Jer 7:4).

The test of our confidence in God is what it produces. If it makes us humble, honest and generous, it is faith. If it lets us go on cheating people while feeling safe, it is superstition.

Therefore because of you Zion shall be plowed as a field; Jerusalem shall become a heap of ruins, and the mountain of the house a wooded height.

This was a shocking thing to say in Jerusalem. The temple hill, the mountain of the house, will become scrubland, and the city a heap of ruins, with farmers plowing where Zion stood. Because of you: the leaders' corruption will bring the city down.

Two things happened to this sentence, and both matter. First, people listened. A hundred years later, when Jeremiah was on trial for saying something similar, the elders quoted this very verse and recalled that Hezekiah had feared the LORD and repented, so that God relented, and Jerusalem was spared in Micah's day (Jer 26:18-19). One sermon, received in repentance, bought a century.

Second, when the warning was finally ignored, it came true. In 586 BC the Babylonians burned the temple and left the city in ruins. God's patience is long, but it is not endless, and the warning nobody acts on is eventually fulfilled.

3.title: Zion Shall Be Plowed as a Field
3.overview:
Micah summons the heads and rulers of Israel, whose task is to know justice, and charges them with hating good and loving evil, tearing the skin from God's people and chopping them up like meat in a pot (vv. 1-3). When they cry to the LORD he will not answer them, but will hide his face, because of their evil deeds (v. 4).

The prophets lead the people astray, crying "Peace" when they are fed and declaring war on those who give them nothing. Therefore it will be night to them, without vision; the sun will go down on the prophets, the seers will be disgraced and cover their lips, for there is no answer from God (vv. 5-7). But Micah is filled with power, with the Spirit of the LORD, with justice and might, to declare to Jacob his transgression (v. 8).

The rulers detest justice and make crooked what is straight, building Zion with blood; its heads judge for a bribe, its priests teach for a price, its prophets divine for money, and still they lean on the LORD and say no disaster will come (vv. 9-11). Therefore Zion will be plowed as a field, Jerusalem become a heap of ruins, and the mountain of the house a wooded height (v. 12).
3.theology:
Authority exists to know and do justice, and God holds leaders accountable for the people entrusted to them (v. 1).

Economic oppression is violence in God's eyes, however respectable its language (vv. 2-3).

Prayer offered without any intention of repenting will not be answered (v. 4; Isa 1:15).

Ministry shaped by money corrupts the message, and God answers it with silence (vv. 5-7; 2 Cor 2:17; 1 Pet 5:2).

The Spirit of the LORD makes his servants truthful rather than popular, and Christ is the supreme example (v. 8; Luke 4:18).

Religious confidence that does not change conduct is superstition, not faith (v. 11; Jer 7:4).

God's warnings are meant to be heeded; heeded, they are relented of, ignored, they are fulfilled (v. 12; Jer 26:18-19).
3.examples:
Judges whose one job is justice, and who hate it.

Oppression described not as policy but as a slaughterhouse.

Prayers from men who intend to change nothing.

A prophet whose message depends on who bought his dinner.

Preachers covering their mouths because heaven has gone quiet.

Fine new buildings with blood in the mortar.

A ploughman working the hill where the temple used to stand.
